newsitem.title: LEBANON: Stranded Iraqi athletes head home.
newsitem.headline: Stranded Iraqi athletes head home.

text.p: Iraqi athletes stranded for two days at the Lebanese border headed home on Saturday after Beirut refused to let them compete in the Pan Arab Games.

As they boarded their buses for the 20-hour return journey to Baghdad, the 97 athletes flourished posters of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein and chanted: "The games without Iraq symbolise rift, revenge and division".

They left this dusty border post on the Syrian-Lebanese frontier just before 7.30 p.m. (1630 GMT) after waiting nearly 36 hours in vain for official word from Lebanon on whether or not they could compete in the games.

As they left, 50,000 spectators gathered at a brand new sports stadium in Beirut, the Lebanese capital, for the opening ceremony of the Pan Arab Games in which 3,000 athletes from 19 countries will compete for the next two weeks.

Lebanese authorities, who excluded Iraq under pressure from its Gulf War foes Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, turned a deaf ear to a demand by the Iraqi delegation leader Assil Tabra for formal notification that the team was being barred or accepted.
Some of the Iraqi athletes, who spent the previous night sleeping on the ground outside the Lebanese immigration hall, expressed deep disappointment at being unable to compete in the games.

"I feel angry and bitter as if there is a fire burning inside me," athlete Mazen Hameed told Reuters. "I wanted so much to take part in these games. After this long trip, we're going back home. What a waste of time."
Journalists overheard delegation leader Tabra complaining to an immigration officer about the Lebanese authorities. "They did not even bother to send an official delegate to apologise," he said.
"We are not begging for participation but we believe it is a right granted to us by the Arab League charter," Tabra said.
An Iraqi newspaper on Saturday demanded that a complaint be lodged against Lebanon at the International Court of Justice for refusing to let Iraq compete in the games.

"The (Iraqi) Olympic Committee is required to protect Iraq and its athletes' right by lodging a case at the International Court of Justice against the ad hoc committee of the Pan Arab Games,"al-Baath al-riyadhi (Sports) newspaper said in an editorial.

Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, which are among the most generous Arab financiers of Lebanon's postwar reconstruction and the main contributors to the $50 million cost of the new sports stadium, threatened to boycott the games if Iraq competed, a Lebanese official said on Wednesday.
The Pan Arab Games, which are held every four years, are the first major international event staged in the Lebanese capital since the end of the 1975-90 civil war.
